power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: In addition, we conducted a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis using the powRICLPM package (Mulder, 2023) to estimate power at the achieved analytic sample size. Given the package's bivariate scope and the same sample size for pairs withing a trivariate model, we ran a three-wave RI-CLPM simulation for the one focal pair -achievement goals with error sensitivity -evaluating the cross-lagged paths in both directions under the specified parameter assumptions of Model 2 (since the package cannot account for exogenous variables). These pairwise analyses provide approximate sensitivity estimates and do not represent power for the full trivariate model.

At the achieved analytic sample size (N = 9,676), three waves, and α = .05, Monte Carlo simulations with 2,000 replications estimated power to detect a standardized cross-lagged weak effect of β = .03. For error sensitivity → achievement goals, estimated power was .858 at ICC = .30 and .782 at ICC = .50; for achievement goals → error sensitivity, power was .867 and .789, respectively. When restricting to medium effect of β = .07, for error sensitivity → achievement goals, estimated power was .998 at ICC = .30 and .985 at ICC = .50; for achievement goals → error sensitivity, power was .999 and .985, respectively.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

Students' reactions to errors are increasingly recognized as central to learning processes.

A substantial body of research shows that errors can foster learning by highlighting knowledge gaps and triggering deeper cognitive and metacognitive processing (see e.g., Lubin et al., 2015; Metcalfe et al., 2025; Ruthig et al., 2017; Zhang & Fiorella, 2023).

text.text: However, learners do not benefit from errors automatically, and may rather react to them differently, ranging from seeing them as learning opportunities to perceiving them as threats (Pan et al., 2020; Tulis et al., 2016), with important consequences for achievement (Soncini et al., 2022).

text.text: To account for these differences in how learners respond to errors, recent research has conceptualized error processing as involving a dynamic interplay of affective, motivational, and self-regulatory processes.

Adaptive responses include maintaining motivation, engaging in error analysis, and persisting despite setbacks, whereas maladaptive responses (e.g., in people with high perfectionism) involve avoidance, disengagement, or reduced effort (Tulis et al., 2016).

text.text: Importantly, experimental evidence shows that these responses can be causally shaped by learners' beliefs about errors.

For example, emphasizing the negative consequences of errors reduces persistence and metacognitive engagement, whereas framing errors as learning opportunities promotes effort investment and adaptive regulation (Soncini et al., 2021; Tulis & Dresel, 2025).

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that the effects of errors on learning are mediated by learners' psychological responses rather than by errors per se.

text.text: Studying error sensitivity alongside achievement goals and self-perceived ability can therefore show how students' concerns about mistakes relate to their perceived competence and the goals they pursue: prior research links positive ability self-concepts and mastery goals to more adaptive responses to errors, and performance-avoidance goals to less adaptive responses (e.g., Steuer et al., 2013).

text.text: Although research has begun to examine the links among error sensitivity, motivation, achievement and self-perceptions about ones' ability, the literature remains limited, particularly with respect to the directionality of these relationships and the role of individual differences over time.

The present study addresses this gap by examining the longitudinal relations between error sensitivity, achievement goals, and self-perceived ability in French and mathematics, with a specific focus on directionality of their associations.

Error sensitivity refers to the extent to which individuals react negatively to errors or failure and has been proposed as a key psychological factor that may profoundly shape academic trajectories (e.g., Pekrun, 2024).

text.text: Many students show a notable aversion to making errors, seeing them as threats rather than learning opportunities (Pan et al., 2020).

text.text: Excessive sensitivity to errors, closely related to fear of failure or a high concern over errors and especially in comparison with others, can lead to maladaptive outcomes such as anxiety, avoidance of challenging tasks, or disengagement from learning, which in turn may undermine performance (Giel et al., 2020).

text.text: For example, Johansson et al. (2024), analyzing data from over 200,000 children, found that sequential errors increased the probability that students would disengage from an online learning task, reflecting a decrease in motivation.

text.text: Importantly, there were large individual differences in this effect: some students showed only a small drop in persistence after errors, whereas others were highly sensitive and disengaged quickly after making mistakes.
These individual differences were stable across tasks, suggesting that error sensitivity may reflect a trait-like characteristic.
Yet, as the authors note, "little is known" about why such differences exist or how they develop.
One possible source of differences in error sensitivity may be teacher-and peer-related supports, such as tolerance, constructive analysis, low ridicule, and encouragement of risk-taking.

These supports are often conceptualized as a positive error climate (which could contribute to lower error sensitivity at individual level) and have been studied as predictors of achievement-related variables.

For example, Steuer et al. (2022) found that perceived positive error climate predicted students' affective-motivational adaptivity, with strong standardized effects (β ≈ .48-.55 across subjects; N = 937 students; 48 classrooms).

text.text: Longitudinal evidence further indicates that students' adaptive reactions to errors tend to decline on average across grades, but that a more positive error climate is associated with a less negative developmental trajectory of error-related adaptivity over time (i.e., lower sensitivity to errors; N = 1,641; 69 classes; five waves; Dresel et al., 2025).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that error sensitivity may play a central role in shaping how learners engage with errors and regulate their behavior in response to them.

However, despite its potential importance, little is known about how error sensitivity relates to various components of motivation, such as achievement goals, and self-perceived ability, particularly over time and in terms of the directionality of these associations.
Achievement goals represent a central framework for understanding students' motivation and have been extensively studied in educational psychology.

A widely used conceptualization is the 2 × 2 achievement goal framework, which distinguishes between mastery and performance goals, each with approach and avoidance components (Elliot & McGregor, 2001).
text.formatted: A widely used conceptualization is the 2 × 2 achievement goal framework, which distinguishes between mastery and performance goals, each with approach and avoidance components <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Elliot & McGregor, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, mastery-approach goals reflect a focus on developing competence and mastering tasks, whereas performance-approach goals emphasize demonstrating competence relative to others.

In contrast, mastery-avoidance goals involve concerns about failing to fully understand or master a task, and performance-avoidance goals reflect concerns about appearing incompetent compared to others.
This framework has been particularly useful for capturing the complexity of students' motivational orientations and their distinct implications for learning and achievement (Butera et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This framework has been particularly useful for capturing the complexity of students' motivational orientations and their distinct implications for learning and achievement <ref type="bibr">(Butera et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A large body of research has shown that these goal orientations are differentially associated with students' affect, motivation, and academic outcomes.

Mastery-approach goals are associated with the use of deeper learning strategies, higher intrinsic motivation, and greater academic effort and perseverance, which in turn support better performance (Guo et al., 2023; Kaplan et al., 2002; Katz-Vago & Benita, 2024).

text.text: In contrast, avoidance-oriented goals are consistently associated with less adaptive outcomes.

Both mastery-avoidance and performance-avoidance goals are associated with higher levels of anxiety and disengagement (An et al., 2022; Bruno et al., 2019; C. Darnon et al., 2007; Elliot & McGregor, 2001; but see Senko & Freund, 2015, for positive effect of mastery-avoidance goals).

text.text: Performance-avoidance goals, in particular, have been identified as the least adaptive type, producing maladaptive motivational patterns such as disorganized studying and an increased fear of failure and focus on one's errors (see discussion in Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Moller & Elliot, 2006; Świątkowski & Dompnier, 2021).

text.text: Some evidence suggests that mastery-avoidance goals may share some maladaptive features with performance-avoidance tendencies.

For example, metaanalytic results indicate that both performance-avoidance and mastery-avoidance goals are associated with higher negative affect (worry, dissatisfaction) in students (Baranik et al., 2010; Huang, 2011).

text.text: However, mastery-avoidance goals remain relatively understudied due to the complexity of the construct and concerns regarding its reliability (see Fiévé et al., 2025 for discussion), highlighting the need for further investigation.

text.text: Another meta-analysis further underscores the asymmetry between approach and avoidance orientations, showing that masteryapproach goals were negatively linked with anxiety (-.10), while performance avoidance demonstrated a stronger positive association (r = .25; Diaconu-Gherasim et al., 2024).

text.text: Despite this, to our knowledge, there are no studies that directly investigated the link between achievement goals and error sensitivity.

Taken together, research discussed above suggests that students who are overly worried about errors may also tend to avoid making errors in front of others (performance-avoidance) or avoid failing to achieve full mastery (mastery-avoidance).

Beyond motivational orientations, students' own perceptions of their academic abilityoften termed academic self-concept or self-perceived achievement -have emerged as powerful predictors of educational success.

A growing body of evidence indicates that how students evaluate their competence in academic domains is strongly associated with objective outcomes such as grades (see some discussion in Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A growing body of evidence indicates that how students evaluate their competence in academic domains is strongly associated with objective outcomes such as grades (see some discussion in <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Steinmayr and colleagues (2019) found that students' domain-specific self-concepts in mathematics and language arts were among the strongest predictors of their grades in those subjects, outperforming even their achievement goal orientations in predictive power.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Steinmayr and colleagues (2019)</ref> found that students' domain-specific self-concepts in mathematics and language arts were among the strongest predictors of their grades in those subjects, outperforming even their achievement goal orientations in predictive power.

text.text: Such findings highlight the importance of students' self-beliefs: when learners feel capable and successful academically, they tend to achieve more.

Over the past decades, researchers have increasingly emphasized the role of self-related constructs, recognizing that academic self-perceptions can both drive engagement and reflect prior successes in a reciprocal cycle (see reviews, Marsh & Craven, 2006; Marsh & O'Mara, 2008).

text.text: For example, several meta-analyses of longitudinal relations found that students who perceive themselves as competent (i.e. higher academic self-concept / self-efficacy) tend to achieve better academic results over time, with almost equal effect in the opposite direction -those with higher achievement demonstrated higher academic self-concept later (Huang, 2011; Wu et al., 2021).

text.text: The results revealed a tightly interconnected cluster that included anxiety, error sensitivity, and imposter syndrome.
This cluster was negatively connected to self-perceived ability in mathematics and French, and positively associated with achievement goals.
Notably, mastery-approach goals were directly linked to error sensitivity and self-perceived ability, suggesting that these constructs may be embedded within a broader motivational system.
However, these findings were based on crosssectional data, precluding establishing the directionality of the effects.

It thus remains unclear whether the relations between self-perceived ability and motivational constructs are unidirectional (perceiving oneself as capable in mathematics leading to higher endorsement of mastery achievement goals or vice versa) or reciprocal (a cycle of effects that unravel in time).

A similar question arises for error sensitivity: whether perceiving oneself as academically capable leads to lower error sensitivity and greater endorsement of approach-oriented goals, or whether lower error sensitivity fosters more positive self-perceptions and adaptive motivational orientations over time.
Several theoretical pathways may underlie the relations between error sensitivity, achievement goals, and self-perceived ability; and suggest some directionality of effects.
A first pathway concerns how errors are appraised and emotionally processed.
As suggested by controlvalue theory, competence and value appraisals generate distinct achievement-related emotions, which in turn influence effort, strategy use, and persistence (Pekrun, 2024).
text.formatted: As suggested by controlvalue theory, competence and value appraisals generate distinct achievement-related emotions, which in turn influence effort, strategy use, and persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Pekrun, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, error sensitivity may bias these appraisals, leading students to interpret errors as more threatening and more diagnostic of their ability.

Such interpretations are likely to reduce perceived control and increase anxiety/shame, especially in high-value domains, thereby decreasing both motivation (especially approach aspect of Achievement goals) and self-perceived ability.
A second pathway involves post-error regulation.

In educational error-learning models, maladaptive reactions to errors involve drops in motivation and increases in dysfunctional emotions, whereas adaptive reactions maintain motivation and support regulatory behaviors such as analyzing the error and persisting (Dresel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In educational error-learning models, maladaptive reactions to errors involve drops in motivation and increases in dysfunctional emotions, whereas adaptive reactions maintain motivation and support regulatory behaviors such as analyzing the error and persisting <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dresel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If error sensitivity increases the subjective cost of errors, students may minimize future exposure by avoiding difficult items, reducing helpseeking, or choosing low-risk tasks.
These patterns are consistent with avoidance-oriented motivational profiles and may, over time, reduce learning opportunities (see e.g., a vicious cycle in mathematics anxiety; Wang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These patterns are consistent with avoidance-oriented motivational profiles and may, over time, reduce learning opportunities (see e.g., a vicious cycle in mathematics anxiety; <ref type="bibr">Wang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A third pathway concerns contextual amplification or buffering via classroom error climate.

A positive error climate (teacher tolerance, supportive responses, peer non-ridicule, and constructive analysis) can reframe errors as informative rather than identity-threatening (reducing error sensitivity), increasing risk-taking and sustaining students' affective-motivational adaptivity (Steuer et al., 2022).

text.text: Similarly, higher levels of approached-oriented motivations and selfperceived ability can be protective against errors (e.g., via ego-busting mechanisms, see e.g., research on narcissism being a protective factor against general anxiety; Papageorgiou et al., 2026), and thus result in lower error sensitivity.

text.text: There is also some evidence, coming from electroencephalography (EEG), that provides insights into neuroscientific mechanisms underlying individual differences in error processing and its links with learners' motivation.

Specifically, evidence from studies using event-related potentials (ERPs) suggests that individuals' level of motivation can systematically shape errormonitoring signals (this brain excitability in relation to errors is conceptually close to error sensitivity), especially the error-related negativity (ERN/Ne), and, in some cases, the later error positivity (Pe).

For example, when errors are made more motivationally significant (e.g., via monetary incentives or reward/punishment contexts), ERN amplitudes tend to increase, which is consistent with enhanced performance monitoring when people are trying harder (Maruo et al., 2016; Pailing & Segalowitz, 2004).

text.text: In addition, when individuals become mentally fatigued or disengage over time, ERN amplitude tends to decrease, suggesting reduced investment in monitoring/cognitive control (Boksem et al., 2006).

text.text: To sum, the associations among error sensitivity, achievement goals and self-perceived ability and the directionality of these associations remain unclear.

This gap is critical, as error sensitivity may represent a key mechanism through which students interpret academic challenges and regulate their engagement, with potential implications for both their motivational orientations and their self-perceptions of competence.

The present study addresses this issue by examining for the first time the longitudinal relations among error sensitivity, achievement goals, and selfperceived ability -to assess the directionality of effects.

Based on the reviewed literature, the current study examined whether: RQ1: higher error sensitivity leads to decrease in approachoriented motivations and self-perceived ability; RQ2: error sensitivity function as an antecedent of avoidance-oriented motivation; RQ3: higher levels of motivational orientations-particularly those involving social comparison (e.g., aiming to perform better than others, such as performanceapproach) lead to heightened sensitivity to errors; RQ4: higher levels of avoidance motivations (especially performance -due to it social component) lead to higher error sensitivity; RQ5: error sensitivity is more strongly associated with avoidance-oriented goals than with approach-oriented goals; and RQ6: whether higher self-perceived ability is associated with lower error sensitivity over time, consistent with the idea that more positive self-perceptions may buffer the perceived threat of errors.
The study draws on a large sample of vocational education (VET) students who are often omitted from motivational research (Bardach et al., 2019).

These structural characteristics have been associated with increased risks of school dropout, behavioral difficulties and emotional challenges, including higher anxiety and lower motivation (Arrighi & Gasquet, 2010; Bernard & Troger, 2012; Jellab, 2017; Solberg et al., 2023).

text.text: In such conditions, students may be particularly vulnerable to errors due to more fragile self-perceptions and prior academic difficulties.
As a result, this population provides a particularly informative case for examining how error sensitivity is related to motivational orientations and self-perceived ability over time.

A total of 10,163 students (59% females; age mode: 16) were recruited from 109 vocational schools in France that volunteered to participate in a nationwide multi-lab longitudinal experiment conducted over three years in two cohorts (2017 and 2018) (PROFAN project; see Riant et al., 2024; Rudmann et al., 2024).

text.text: The project aimed to examine the effects of two cooperative learning approaches (Jigsaw classroom and another form of collaborative learning), compared to standard instructional practices.
The data analyzed in the present study were drawn from this larger project and focus on three measurement occasions spanning two academic years.
Participants' age at Time 1 ranged from under 15 to over 20 years, with the majority being 16 years old.

Students were enrolled in three vocational tracks: MELEC (electricity, industrial systems and maintenance; N= 2,441, 1.76% females), ASSP (nursing and care; N= 3,454, 88.85% females), and COMMERCE (sales, promoting and managing retail space; N= 4,268, 49.39 % females).
Given the substantial variation in gender composition across vocational tracks, educational track and gender were accounted for in the analyses.

Socio-economic status (SES) of participants was assessed using the highest level of parental education, with majority of participants coming from families with secondary education (~62%): "Lower-secondary certificate/completed lower secondary education" (6.4%), "Short vocational upper-secondary qualification" (25.1%), and "Upper-secondary school-leaving qualification" (31.12%).
Parents of one third of participants (~30%) had higher education: "Short-cycle tertiary degree/diploma" (19.24%), and "University or other higher-education degree" (11.08%).
7.06% of parents reported that they had "no diploma".

The present study uses data collected at three time points: Time 1 (September-October, beginning of the school year, Grade 11), Time 2 (end of Grade 11), and Time 3 (end of Grade 12).
Time 1 data were collected prior to the implementation of the experimental instructional conditions in classrooms.
The lag between T1 and T2 (~7.4 months) was comparable to the lag between T2 and T3 (~9.4 months).
The ProFAN experimentation was commissioned and authorized by the French Ministry of Education under an official ministerial decree (Arrêté du 21 mars 2017).
Formal participation agreements were signed between each participating school and the corresponding Academic Directorate (Rectorat).
All data were anonymized prior to analysis, and data collection and processing complied with French data-protection regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
Students completed an online survey in school computer rooms, containing multiple scales, a subset of which is analyzed in the current study (see below).
The study included measures of achievement goals, error sensitivity, self-perceived ability in French and mathematics, collected over three time points.
In addition, students provided selfreported grades in these two subjects at Time 1.
All measures were adapted to French, validated and demonstrated sufficient reliability in previous research as well as in the current sample.

text.text: To investigate the longitudinal links among achievement goals, error sensitivity, and selfperceived academic ability measured, we estimated classical Cross-Lagged Panel Models (CLPMs) and more advanced Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPM) across three time points.

CLPM allows to test directional (quasi-causal) hypotheses by estimating whether a variable X predicts later changes in Y above and beyond prior levels of Y, while simultaneously testing the reverse path (Lüdtke & Robitzsch, 2022; Selig & Little, 2012).
text.formatted: CLPM allows to test directional (quasi-causal) hypotheses by estimating whether a variable X predicts later changes in Y above and beyond prior levels of Y, while simultaneously testing the reverse path <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Lüdtke & Robitzsch, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Selig & Little, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The lagged paths are essential because they impose temporal precedence and control for autoregressive stability, allowing the cross-lagged coefficients to approximate prospective influence rather than mere contemporaneous association.

Given ongoing methodological discussions regarding limitations of traditional Cross-Lagged Panel Models, including their inability to disentangle stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations over time (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015; Orth et al., 2021), we additionally estimated Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPMs; Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Given ongoing methodological discussions regarding limitations of traditional Cross-Lagged Panel Models, including their inability to disentangle stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations over time (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hamaker et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Orth et al., 2021)</ref>, we additionally estimated Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPMs; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: RI-CLPMs separate stable between-person variance from within-person deviations around individuals' expected levels, thereby allowing a more precise examination of temporal withinperson processes.

Consequently, the estimated autoregressive and cross-lagged effects reflect whether changes in one variable relative to an individual's typical level predict subsequent changes in another variable, rather than conflating these dynamics with stable differences between individuals.

The size of lagged effects is typically evaluated using standardized coefficients, confidence intervals, and explained variance, interpreted relative to autoregressive paths and emerging empirical benchmarks (e.g., small ≈ .03, medium ≈ .07, large ≈ .12), alongside robustness checks across alternative models (Orth et al., 2024).

text.text: The traditional CLPMs consistently indicated reciprocal prospective associations between achievement goals and error sensitivity, with small effects in both directions (β = [0.05-0.14]).
The path from error sensitivity to mastery-avoidance (Panel D) was, however, somewhat stronger than for the other goals (β coefficient = 0.14).
In contrast, the associations between selfperceived ability and achievement goals were predominantly unidirectional.

Self-perceived academic ability positively predicted subsequent mastery-approach (Panel A; β coefficient = .08), performance-approach (Panel B; 0.12), and mastery-avoidance goals (Panel C; 0.06), but not performance-avoidance goals (Panel D).

The reverse paths-from achievement goals to subsequent self-perceived ability-are uniformly negligible (β = [0.01-0.02]), with a small negative effect observed only for mastery-avoidance (Panel D; -0.02).

Finally, associations between error sensitivity and self-perceived ability were generally weak or non-significant across panels, suggesting that their link did not play a substantial role in the longitudinal dynamics observed.
Thus, unlike the RI-CLPMs, the traditional CLPMs suggested reciprocal prospective associations between error sensitivity and achievement goals.
This discrepancy is considered further in the Discussion.

The current study examined the directionality of connections among the four achievement goals, self-perceived ability, and error sensitivity in a large sample of vocational education students.

At the between-person level, error sensitivity, self-perceived academic ability, and achievement goals were strongly associated.
At the within-person level, however, prospective associations were small, mostly unidirectional, and did not support a general reciprocal cycle between error sensitivity and achievement goals.

Specifically, positive within-person variations in prior error sensitivity and self-perceived ability predicted modest subsequent increases in mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performance-approach goals.
These three goals did not, in turn, predict subsequent changes in error sensitivity or self-perceived academic ability.

Performance-avoidance goals showed a different pattern: they were predicted by neither prior error sensitivity nor self-perceived ability, but they predicted a small subsequent decrease in error sensitivity.
A noteworthy finding concerns the different conclusions produced by traditional CLPMs and RI-CLPM.
Traditional CLPMs showed positive reciprocal links between achievement goals and error sensitivity.
However, these reciprocal paths disappeared in the RI-CLPM after stable between-person differences were separated from within-person variations.

This discrepancy suggests that the apparent reciprocal links identified by the traditional CLPMs probably reflect differences between students (that were captured by relatively high correlations between random intercepts in RI-CLPM), rather than "true" causal effects from on time point to another (see Hamaker et al., 2015 for discussion of such effects).

text.text: Importantly, the traditional CLPM results were theoretically plausible and could be interpreted as reflecting a self-reinforcing cycle in which heightened sensitivity to errors strengthens goal striving, which, in turn, amplifies emotional reactions to errors (Daniels et al., 2009).

text.text: The RI-CLPM results indicated that this theoretically compelling interpretation was not supported at the within-person level.
This illustrates the importance of distinguishing between-person differences from within-person variations before drawing conclusions about reciprocal longitudinal associations.
For this reason, the following discussion is based on the RI-CLPM results.
Between-person links between achievement goals, error sensitivity and self-perceived ability
The strong positive between-person associations between the four achievement goals and error sensitivity are consistent with prior cross-sectional research.

Endorsing achievement goals, especially avoidance-oriented goals for which the associations with error sensitivity were stronger (.57-.69 vs. .45-.53 for approach goals -partly supporting prediction of RQ5), may increase the perceived stakes of success and failure, thereby making errors more salient and emotionally charged (e.g., Giel et al., 2020).

text.text: Conversely, students who are highly sensitive to errors may adopt multiple achievement goals as strategies for coping with the possibility of failure.

Self-perceived ability correlated with most goals weakly and positively (.04-.17 -highest correlation with mastery approach), with only exception being mastery avoidance goals for which correlation was negative (-.07); and with error sensitivity negatively and weakly (-.08).

From a perfectionism perspective, these associations suggest that error sensitivity may be embedded in a broader dispositional system involving chronic self-evaluation, perceived competence, and standards for defining success and failure (see clusters resulted from network analysis in; Likhanov, Fillon, et al., 2026).

text.text: For example, concern over mistakes has been shown to reflect not only dislike of errors but also a tendency to equate them with personal failure and anticipated negative judgment from others (Smith et al., 2022a).

text.text: Self-perceived academic ability may constitute another component of this system, as academic self-concept covaries with motivation and performance over time.

Thus, at the between-person level, it is theoretically plausible that students who generally feel more competent, but are also more vigilant about mistakes, would report stronger and more differentiated achievement-goal profiles than peers with lower standing on these constructs (e.g., Steinberg et al., 2024).

text.text: Such a pattern also suggests that concerns over mistakes, academic self-beliefs, and goal orientations may cluster together in meaningful ways.

For example, perfectionistic profiles characterized by stronger evaluative concerns, especially when combined with family pressure, have been associated with greater endorsement of performance-avoidance and work-avoidance goals.
In contrast, high standards without the same level of external pressure aligned more with mastery-approach goals and stronger academic performance (Fang & Sotardi, 2026).

text.text: Although the within-person effects were much smaller than the between-person associations, they are theoretically quite informative and supplement the results above by suggesting some directionality to the links discussed above.
First, higher prior error sensitivity predicted modest subsequent increases in mastery-avoidance, mastery-approach, and performance-approach goals.

Thus, changes in students' sensitivity to errors were followed by small changes in their motivation to develop competence, avoid failing to master a task, or demonstrate competence relative to others, suggesting that higher error sensitivity may not be purely debilitating -contradicting our prediction on higher error sensitivity leading to decrease in approach oriented motivations (RQ1); supporting the claim that error sensitivity will contribute to avoidance-oriented motivations (RQ2) and contradicting our prediction of higher levels of motivation (particularly performance-approach) leading to heightened sensitivity to error (RQ3).

This interpretation, however, fits contemporary perfectionism theory, which distinguishes high standards from maladaptive evaluative concerns while recognizing that the two often co-occur in students (Smith et al., 2022b).

text.text: When a student becomes temporarily more alert to the consequences of error, that state may activate a wish both to improve the self and to demonstrate competence, especially when this still feels controllable.

Recent research similarly indicates that personal standards and perfectionistic concerns can jointly shape mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performance-approach goals through distinct pathways (e.g., Cecalupo et al., 2026).

text.text: In this sense, heightened error sensitivity may function as a short-term catalyst for intensified striving, even if its long-run costs are substantial.
It should be noted that the changes in error sensitivity were followed only by modest changes in achievement goals, and the reverse paths were not supported (unlike in regular CLPM).

Such small effects are expected in RI-CLPM logic (Hamaker et al., 2015): once stable individual differences are partialled out, the remaining wave-to-wave deviations in motivational states are usually subtle.

performance opposition, suggested by RQ4.
Second, self-perceived academic ability showed a similar asymmetric pattern.

Higher prior selfperceived ability predicted subsequent increases in mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performance-approach goals (RQ6), whereas none of the four goals predicted subsequent changes in self-perceived ability.
Feeling more competent may therefore increase students' willingness to invest in achievement and pursue a range of competence-related standards.

This finding is broadly consistent with previous research showing that feeling capable promotes stronger endorsement of achievement goals, particularly approach-oriented goals (Ciani et al., 2011; Moller & Elliot, 2006; Seaton et al., 2014).

text.text: The absence of reverse paths may reflect the high temporal stability of perceived competence and its strong dependence on prior achievement and evaluative feedback.

Controlling for baseline competence, as in the present study, substantially reduces the variance available for achievement goals to explain subsequent changes in self-perceived ability (Marsh & Craven, 2006; Niepel et al., 2014).

text.text: A distinct pattern for performance-avoidance goals: a defensive mechanism against social comparison and stress in relation to errors?
Unlike the other three achievement goals, Performance-avoidance goals were predicted by neither prior error sensitivity nor prior self-perceived ability.

More strikingly, performanceavoidance was the only achievement goal to predict subsequent error sensitivity (supporting prediction of RQ4): at the within-person level, higher prior performance-avoidance predicted a small decrease in subsequent error sensitivity.
At first glance, this negative path seems counterintuitive.

Given that performance-avoidance goals are generally associated with greater anxiety and internalizing symptoms, lower intrinsic motivation, and poorer achievement outcomes (Diaconu-Gherasim et al., 2024; Möcklinghoff et al., 2023), one might have expected stronger performance-avoidance to heighten students' vigilance towards mistakes and thereby increase, rather than decrease, subsequent error sensitivity.
text.formatted: Given that performance-avoidance goals are generally associated with greater anxiety and internalizing symptoms, lower intrinsic motivation, and poorer achievement outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Diaconu-Gherasim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Möcklinghoff et al., 2023)</ref>, one might have expected stronger performance-avoidance to heighten students' vigilance towards mistakes and thereby increase, rather than decrease, subsequent error sensitivity.

text.text: One possible explanation is that increased performance-avoidance promotes defensive disengagement from error-related information.

Because students high in performance-avoidance goals are motivated to avoid appearing incompetent, attending closely to their mistakes may expose them to precisely the evidence of low ability and negative evaluation that they seek to avoid.
They may therefore reduce their vigilance towards errors, process them less deeply, or withdraw from evaluative situations in which such errors become salient.
This interpretation is supported by several lines of research.

For example, one of the classical studies on achievement goals showed that students high in performance-avoidance goals tend to rely more on surface-level and disorganized study strategies, rather than deep processing, which may make errors less likely to be used as informative feedback for learning (Elliot, 1999).

text.text: The current study has a number of limitations.
First, the data were collected in the context of an educational intervention, which may have affected the variables and their longitudinal associations.

However, experimental conditions showed negligible effects in previous studies (e.g., Riant et al., 2024) and were therefore statistically controlled -brining no meaningful differences in lagged paths in the current study.
text.formatted: However, experimental conditions showed negligible effects in previous studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Riant et al., 2024)</ref> and were therefore statistically controlled -brining no meaningful differences in lagged paths in the current study.

text.text: Second, the temporal design warrants consideration.
The time intervals between measurement waves were unequal, which could have affected the magnitude of cross-lag effects.
To address this, we equalized the cross-lag loadings, which resulted in improved model fit and suggested that the effects were stable across time.
In addition, the study included three measurement occasions, the minimum required to estimate an RI-CLPM (Hamaker et al., 2015; Mulder & Hamaker, 2021).
text.formatted: In addition, the study included three measurement occasions, the minimum required to estimate an RI-CLPM <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hamaker et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Mulder & Hamaker, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although sufficient for model estimation, three waves provide only a limited representation of within-person dynamics and may not capture more transient or complex patterns of change.
Another related issue is that Mathematics and French grades were available only at T1, precluding investigation of their cross-lag effects.
Future longitudinal studies including more measurement occasions and repeated measures of achievement would allow a more detailed and stable characterization of these dynamics.
Third, mathematics and French selfperceived ability scores were averaged to create a domain-general measure, consistent with the domain-general assessment of achievement goals and error sensitivity.
However, this aggregation may have obscured domain-specific effects, which have been documented in prior research (e.g., Fiévé et al., 2025; Susperreguy et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, this aggregation may have obscured domain-specific effects, which have been documented in prior research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fiévé et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Susperreguy et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This loss of domain specificity might partly explain the absence of reciprocal associations between achievement goals and self-perceived academic ability.
Fourth, the RI-CLPM analyses were based on total scale scores rather than item-level latent variables.
This may have affected the estimates by ignoring measurement error and potential itemlevel heterogeneity.
To address this concern, we applied a correction based on composite reliability at each wave, following (Kline, 2016).
text.formatted: To address this concern, we applied a correction based on composite reliability at each wave, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kline, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We also estimated item-level models, but they failed to fit adequately, likely due to their substantially greater complexity.
Reliability-corrected composite scores therefore provided a reasonable compromise between accounting for measurement error and maintaining model parsimony.
The within-person associations remained small, and their theoretical and practical significance should not be overstated.

Effects of this magnitude are yet common when stable between-person differences are separated from within-person variations (Hamaker et al., 2015), but future studies using fully latent models are needed to obtain more precise estimates.

text.text: Confidence in the main findings is strengthened by the consistency of the overall pattern across achievement goals, experimental conditions, and analyses including versus excluding outliers.
Finally, gender and educational track were included as covariates, but their potential moderating effects were not examined due to unbalanced group compositions.

This limits our ability to determine whether the longitudinal associations differ across these groups, despite previous evidence of moderation by gender and educational track (Likhanov, Fillon, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This limits our ability to determine whether the longitudinal associations differ across these groups, despite previous evidence of moderation by gender and educational track <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Likhanov, Fillon, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, including both variables as covariates allowed the main estimates to account for mean-level differences associated with these group characteristics.
Despite these limitations, the present study has several important methodological, theoretical, and practical implications.
At the methodological level, the contrast between traditional CLPMs and RI-CLPMs demonstrates that the choice of longitudinal model can substantially alter the conclusions drawn.

Previous cross-sectional and two-wave studies may yield associations consistent with theoretically plausible bidirectional relations, and traditional CLPMs can further reinforce this interpretation by producing reciprocal cross-lagged paths.

However, such converging evidence does not establish that these processes unfold within individuals, because these designs do not adequately separate stable between-person differences from within-person variations.

The present findings illustrate the added value of the RI-CLPM: reciprocal associations between error sensitivity and achievement goals disappeared once these two sources of variance were distinguished.
This methodological issue extends beyond the constructs examined here.

Recent research on academic self-concept and achievement similarly shows that conclusions about reciprocal relations depend on separating stable and dynamic components and on aligning model specifications with the timescale of the underlying processes (Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2026).

text.text: This does not imply that RI-CLPMs should invariably replace traditional CLPMs; rather, different models capture different sources and timescales of variation and should not be interpreted interchangeably (Hamaker et al., 2015; Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2026).

text.text: At the theoretical level, ruling out a general reciprocal within-person process changes how the relations among achievement goals, error sensitivity, and self-perceived academic ability should be conceptualized.

Rather than forming a self-reinforcing motivational system, these constructs appear to follow an asymmetric organization in which perceived competence and sensitivity to errors contribute to subsequent goal endorsement, whereas there was no evidence that achievement goals directly predict subsequent changes in these beliefs and error-related responses.

One possible interpretation is that achievement goals influence perceived competence and error sensitivity only indirectly, through the experiences associated with goal pursuit, such as engagement, goal attainment, success or failure, and evaluative feedback (Arens et al., 2017; Hübner et al., 2025; Theobald et al., 2023).

text.text: These potential pathways were not examined in the present study and should be tested in future longitudinal research.
The contrast between performance-avoidance and the other three goals also suggests a possible refinement of the 2 × 2 achievement-goal framework.

Although mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performanceapproach goals occupy different positions within this framework, they showed the same general pattern of longitudinal associations, possibly because they all involve continued investment in attaining, maintaining, or demonstrating competence.
Performance-avoidance goals showed a distinct pattern and may instead involve protecting the self from evidence of incompetence by disengaging from errors and threatening evaluative information.

Achievement-goal theory may therefore benefit from considering not only how competence is defined and valenced, but also whether students remain actively engaged with competence-relevant information or defensively withdraw from it.
These theoretical implications, in turn, inform several practical recommendations.

Because self-perceived academic ability preceded stronger endorsement of three achievement goals, teachers may support students' motivation by creating credible experiences of competence through appropriately challenging tasks, progressive scaffolding, opportunities to improve, and feedback that makes individual progress visible (Belland et al., 2013; Jang et al., 2010; Ryan & Deci, 2020).
text.formatted: Because self-perceived academic ability preceded stronger endorsement of three achievement goals, teachers may support students' motivation by creating credible experiences of competence through appropriately challenging tasks, progressive scaffolding, opportunities to improve, and feedback that makes individual progress visible <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Belland et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Jang et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Ryan & Deci, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, strengthening perceived competence should not be expected, by itself, to produce more constructive responses to errors.
Similarly, promoting adaptive achievement goals-even masteryapproach goals-may benefit engagement and learning but is unlikely to be sufficient to change how students respond to mistakes.
Error processing should therefore be addressed directly.

Teachers can ask students to identify the source of an error, explain the reasoning that produced it, compare alternative strategies, correct their response, and apply what they have learned in a subsequent attempt.

At the same time, they should reduce classroom conditions that foster performance-avoidance, including public social comparison, excessive emphasis on normative evaluation, and feedback that presents errors as indicators of low ability.
Framing errors as informative and revisable and providing feedback privately when appropriate may help students remain engaged with potentially threatening information.

These practices could reduce defensive disengagement without encouraging indifference to mistakes, while supporting both students' sense of competence and their constructive use of errors (Steuer et al., 2022; Tulis & Dresel, 2025).
text.formatted: These practices could reduce defensive disengagement without encouraging indifference to mistakes, while supporting both students' sense of competence and their constructive use of errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Steuer et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Tulis & Dresel, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Given the small longitudinal effects and observational design of the study, these recommendations should nevertheless be tested directly in classroom interventions.
The present study investigated the longitudinal associations among achievement goals, error sensitivity, and self-perceived academic ability.
The findings from traditional CLPM suggested that they form a reciprocal, self-reinforcing motivational system.

However, once stable differences between persons were separated from within-person variations in RI-CLPM, their longitudinal relations proved selective and asymmetric, with performance-avoidance showing a particularly distinct pattern.

More broadly, adaptive motivation cannot be inferred from stronger goal endorsement or lower error sensitivity alone, but should be understood in terms of students' continued and constructive engagement with competence-relevant feedback.
